title: object, Common Type System, and dynamic (late binding)
hook: Every C# type ultimately connects to `object` through the Common Type System (CTS). `dynamic` is different — it tells the compiler to figure out members at run time, like a safety-off switch.

blocks.text: The **Common Type System (CTS)** is the rulebook that says every type in .NET inherits from `System.Object` (written `object` in C#). Value types inherit `System.ValueType`, which itself inherits `object`. That is why a `List<object>` can hold an `int` (via **boxing**) and a `string` side by side. **`dynamic`** is not a new type — it tells the compiler to defer member lookup to the **Dynamic Language Runtime (DLR)** binder at run time. Typos compile; they throw at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET rule set that unifies types across languages. Every type derives from `object` and can be described with common metadata.
entries.example: C#, F#, and Visual Basic types can interoperate because they follow the CTS.

entries.plainDefinition: The root reference type. Variables typed `object` can hold any value, but you must cast or test before using specific members.
entries.example: `object boxed = 199;` — the `int` is boxed into an `object` reference.

entries.plainDefinition: A compile-time hint that member access is resolved at run time by the DLR. Errors that `object` would catch at compile time slip through until execution.
entries.example: `dynamic d = GetJson(); d.nme.ToString();` — compiles, throws at run time (typo in `nme`).

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET component that resolves `dynamic` member calls at run time. Adds overhead and a dependency on `Microsoft.CSharp`.
entries.example: Used when calling COM objects or some JSON APIs — prefer typed DTOs instead.

blocks.text: Heterogeneous logging (`List<object>`) is convenient but boxes value types and costs allocations. JSON from an auth provider should deserialize into a typed DTO (`AuthToken`), not a `dynamic` blob. In interviews, saying C# has TypeScript `any` is wrong — say `object` (static, needs cast) or `dynamic` (late binding). TypeScript `unknown` forces narrowing; C# has no `unknown` keyword — use `object` plus `is` patterns.

blocks.title: object vs dynamic
blocks.body: `object`: compile-time type is `object` — the compiler blocks `.Length` until you cast. `dynamic`: compile-time checks are skipped — the DLR resolves at run time and throws on failure.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: From value to object and back

items.title: Assign a value type to object
items.body: The runtime **boxes** the value — copies it into a heap object. `object o = 42;`

items.title: Use the value
items.body: With `object`, you must cast or pattern-match: `if (o is int n) Use(n);`

items.title: Or declare dynamic
items.body: `dynamic d = o;` — the compiler emits DLR calls for `d.SomeMethod()` without knowing `SomeMethod` exists.

items.title: Prefer generics over both
items.body: `List<int>` avoids boxing. A typed DTO avoids `dynamic` entirely.

diagram.title: CTS hierarchy and dynamic binding
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  OBJ["object (CTS root)"]
  OBJ --> VT["ValueType"]
  OBJ --> CLS["class types (string, List)"]
  VT --> INT["int, bool, decimal, struct..."]
  INT -->|box| BOX["object wrapper on heap"]
  DYN["dynamic variable"] -->|"DLR binder at run time"| CALL["Member call resolved late"]

snippet.label: object needs a test; dynamic fails late
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: `object` holds a boxed `int`; `is int n` unboxes safely. Line 11: `object` only exposes `object` members at compile time — custom methods need a cast to a derived type.

snippet.label: dynamic compiles, throws at run time
snippet.explanation: Line 4: `dynamic` skips compile-time member checking — `nme` is a typo for `name`. Line 7: `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<AuthToken>` gives compile-time safety and IntelliSense. Prefer DTOs over `dynamic` for auth tokens.

snippet.label: Heterogeneous list vs generic
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `List<object>` boxes the `int` and `decimal`. Line 5: `List<int>` stores unboxed integers. Line 8: when you must use `object`, immediately narrow with `is`.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `dynamic` for JSON because it "feels like JavaScript." Storing value types in `object` collections and creating boxing traffic in hot paths. Saying C# has `any` — it does not; say `object` or `dynamic` and explain the difference.

interviewTakeaways: CTS: one object hierarchy; boxing is how values enter it.
`object` is statically typed as object; you must convert to use members.
`dynamic` is compile-time `object`-ish with run-time binding — closer to `any` than to `unknown`, but still a .NET DLR feature.
commonPitfalls: Using `dynamic` for JSON because it "feels like JS."
Storing value types in `object` collections and creating boxing traffic.
Saying C# has `any` — it does not; say `object` or `dynamic` and know the difference.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript `any` skips checks and erases. `unknown` must be narrowed. C# `object` is a real type you cast; `dynamic` skips member checks but still runs on the CLR DLR binder.
